rv.q: Memon proceeds to do just that, setting the theatre alight (metaphorically!) as she relives Ria's tale with scorching, heartfelt passion.
It's Memon's performance, oozing warmth and charisma, that makes this exceptionally crafted piece of gig theatre soar.
Manic Street Creature is a calling card for Memon’s considerable array of talents.
But there’s no escaping that the storyline piles one cliché on another, and the way the show addresses mental health issues is earnest but trite.
Memon is a performer of astonishingly varied and endless talents.
She is vivid, she is real, and she is alive in an astounding piece of musical theatre.
It absolutely does as a compelling, emotionally resonant showcase of Memon's skill as both a performer and storyteller.

The material possesses moments of gentle comedy and touching pathos, most of all it has an inherent humanity and subtly asks us to consider the stark realities of mental health issues from different angles and perspectives.
The emotional intensity rarely lets up and, at more than ninety minutes without interval, that becomes demanding.
Memon triumphs in articulating a tale of true despair and hope.
The songs are wonderful and tell the story so clearly; it just felt like a few more songs instead of the spoken word towards the end could have really rocked the piece.

cn.t: Memon's semi-autobiographical gig theatre showcases her formidable vocals and folk-infused sound, though critics are mixed on whether the personal mental health narrative fully matches the musical firepower.
